subject: When does the data dominates the posterior distribution?

messages.author: c80c69de54446223
messages.subject: When does the data dominates the posterior distribution?
parts:
Hi everyone,

I have a probably naive question but I did not find a proper answer anywhere, so I apologize in advance.

I have a time series on which I estimate a parameter (beta), and I want to know at which point in time does the data dominates the posterior distribution of my parameters (or in other words, at which point does the prior distribution not matter anymore). So my idea was to fit the model n times using data available until each date, and to measure the KL divergence between the prior and the posterior distribution computed at each point. I expect the KL divergence to be small at first when little data is provided, and to increase up to a plateau, at which point the posterior distribution depends mainly on the data.

1/ Is that a proper way to answer my question?

2/ I feel that my way of computing the KL-divergence is kind of rustic (using the nearest neighbor algorithm of package FNN), could someone confirm that this is correct (in particular considering the parameter k)?

library(FNN)
beta_P <- rexp(length(R0_Q),rate=0.5) # my weakly informative prior distribution (exponential with rate 1/2), I follow a similar method with informative priors in another approach
beta_Q <- extract(S_D1_NIP,pars="beta")[[1]] # extract the posterior distribution

mean(KL.divergence(beta_P ,beta_Q ,k=10)

I hope that I was clear enough.

Thanks in advance!
Julien

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] When does the data dominates the posterior distribution?
parts:
This is good to think about for understanding, but in practice, isn't very useful. We just want to put in a prior based on what we know. It's just as much a part of the model as the likelihood, and we don't want to be thinking in terms of how we code it so it gets washed out.

You might be able to get a decent feel for what's going on with a simple conjugate example (let's say normal with fixed variance or a beta distribution). You can see that where the prior starts and how much it's concentrated matters. Michael Betancourt's about to roll out a nice case study where you can see how much the fatness of the prior's tails (Cauchy vs. normal, say) and the consistency of the prior (is the posterior concentrating in the trunk or the tails) make a big difference.

No idea about FNN. KL-divergence requires computing an integral, which you
can compute in one direction with MCMC if you have draws from the posterior and
an analytic prior. But you're probably better served by plotting out the
priors and posteriors and seeing how the latter concentrate as a function of
the prior and amount of data (and the variance in the data itself).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] When does the data dominates the posterior distribution?
parts:
Hi Bob, thank you for your time!

I get why this is not very useful in general, however in this particular case (epidemic data) it is important because I want to determine the earliest date at which we can produce reliable estimates (and whether using informative priors allow to produce estimates at an earlier date, which is always good when epidemics are ongoing). Informative priors are rarely used in my field, and we're doing a sort of simulation study to highlitght the advantages.

So using a conjugate example won't help much here, as I already have a model that I'm interested in. I already plotted the posterior and prior distributions and it works as intended, but I would like a measure of divergence to systematically compare my (numerous) models. I take from your point that I could include the computation of the KL divergence directly in Stan (maybe in the generated quantities)?

Best regards,
Julien

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] When does the data dominates the posterior distribution?
parts:
You cannot accurately estimate the KL divergence between the prior
and the posterior using posterior samples.  In general KL divergences
are incredibly difficult to estimate at all and hence they are of extremely
limited empirical use.  Ultimately there is little to be learned from trying
to quantify the qualitative results that you already have.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] When does the data dominates the posterior distribution?
parts:
What do you mean by "a reliable estimate"?

Everything we're talking about here is model internal. May I suggest
not putting so much trust in your model and rather going out and
trying to measure your models predictive calibration with real data?
Then you can start measuring the things you really care about.

- Bob

P.S. I now see the problem with computing KL---we can't get the
normalizing term for the posterior density, which we need in the
expectation term.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] When does the data dominates the posterior distribution?
parts:
It's trivial to show you get better inference with priors. Just
set the prior to the posterior you'd get after seeing a lot of data.

To do this more realistically, what you care about is calibration of
your predictive intervals (so that when you say something is 50% likely
to fall in an interval, it falls in that interval 50% of the time [plus
or minus sampling error --- you expect binomial(N, 0.5) for N
50% interval tests]). Once you're calibrated, you care about sharpness.
How narrow are the intervals? Or if you're thinking of doing probabilistic
predictions of event probabilities, how close are those estimates to 0 or
1?

I really like this Gneiting et al. paper on these topics and wonder
why things are presented this way more often in Bayesin stats:

Probabilistic forecasts, calibration and sharpness.
https://www.stat.washington.edu/raftery/Research/PDF/Gneiting2007jrssb.pdf

- Bob

> On Mar 2, 2017, at 1:28 AM, Julien Riou <julien...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Sorry I was not clear enough. I'm already doing just what you say, and measure the predictive capabilities of the models at each point in time with real data (and that's indeed how I know when I obtain a "reliable estimate"). But you see, as I want to show that using informative priors allows to obtain better estimate at earlier dates (which is kind of obvious for many here but is unusual in my field), I'd like to have a concrete measure of how my priors and data interact, and whether data contradicts the prior distribution in some cases.
>
>
> On Thursday, March 2, 2017 at 3:37:21 AM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> What do you mean by "a reliable estimate"?
>
> Everything we're talking about here is model internal. May I suggest
> not putting so much trust in your model and rather going out and
> trying to measure your models predictive calibration with real data?
> Then you can start measuring the things you really care about.
>
> - Bob
>
> P.S. I now see the problem with computing KL---we can't get the
> normalizing term for the posterior density, which we need in the
> expectation term.
>
>
> > On Mar 1, 2017, at 2:59 AM, Julien Riou <julien...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Bob, thank you for your time!
> >
> > I get why this is not very useful in general, however in this particular case (epidemic data) it is important because I want to determine the earliest date at which we can produce reliable estimates (and whether using informative priors allow to produce estimates at an earlier date, which is always good when epidemics are ongoing). Informative priors are rarely used in my field, and we're doing a sort of simulation study to highlitght the advantages.
> >
> > So using a conjugate example won't help much here, as I already have a model that I'm interested in. I already plotted the posterior and prior distributions and it works as intended, but I would like a measure of divergence to systematically compare my (numerous) models. I take from your point that I could include the computation of the KL divergence directly in Stan (maybe in the generated quantities)?
> >
> > Best regards,
> > Julien
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > On Tuesday, February 28, 2017 at 8:52:49 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > This is good to think about for understanding, but in practice, isn't very useful. We just want to put in a prior based on what we know. It's just as much a part of the model as the likelihood, and we don't want to be thinking in terms of how we code it so it gets washed out.
> >
> > You might be able to get a decent feel for what's going on with a simple conjugate example (let's say normal with fixed variance or a beta distribution). You can see that where the prior starts and how much it's concentrated matters. Michael Betancourt's about to roll out a nice case study where you can see how much the fatness of the prior's tails (Cauchy vs. normal, say) and the consistency of the prior (is the posterior concentrating in the trunk or the tails) make a big difference.
> >
> > No idea about FNN. KL-divergence requires computing an integral, which you
> > can compute in one direction with MCMC if you have draws from the posterior and
> > an analytic prior. But you're probably better served by plotting out the
> > priors and posteriors and seeing how the latter concentrate as a function of
> > the prior and amount of data (and the variance in the data itself).
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > > On Feb 28, 2017, at 5:54 AM, Julien Riou <julien...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Hi everyone,
> > >
> > > I have a probably naive question but I did not find a proper answer anywhere, so I apologize in advance.
> > >
> > > I have a time series on which I estimate a parameter (beta), and I want to know at which point in time does the data dominates the posterior distribution of my parameters (or in other words, at which point does the prior distribution not matter anymore). So my idea was to fit the model n times using data available until each date, and to measure the KL divergence between the prior and the posterior distribution computed at each point. I expect the KL divergence to be small at first when little data is provided, and to increase up to a plateau, at which point the posterior distribution depends mainly on the data.
> > >
> > > 1/ Is that a proper way to answer my question?
> > >
> > > 2/ I feel that my way of computing the KL-divergence is kind of rustic (using the nearest neighbor algorithm of package FNN), could someone confirm that this is correct (in particular considering the parameter k)?
> > >
> > > library(FNN)
> > > beta_P <- rexp(length(R0_Q),rate=0.5) # my weakly informative prior distribution (exponential with rate 1/2), I follow a similar method with informative priors in another approach
> > > beta_Q <- extract(S_D1_NIP,pars="beta")[[1]] # extract the posterior distribution
> > >
> > > mean(KL.divergence(beta_P ,beta_Q ,k=10)
> > >
> > > I hope that I was clear enough.
> > >
> > > Thanks in advance!
> > > Julien

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] When does the data dominates the posterior distribution?
parts:
Hi Bob, thanks again for taking the time!

Regarding the triviality of my objective, I assure you that in my setting it makes sense! Basically, I'm modelling Zika virus epidemics in several areas using surveillance data. In epidemic situations, it is very important to be able to predict the outcome (duration, peak date, final attack rate) as early as possible. There are several methods for that, which are all frequentist or using flat priors. The thing is, it's an emerging epidemic, so we don't have much prior data. What I'm trying to do is to use previous Chikungunya epidemics in the same areas to build a prior distribution for the Zika epidemic, and to show that using this prior improves the epidemic assessment (i.e. its reliability at early stages of the epidemic). This is assuming that Zika and Chikungunya epidemics follow the same pattern (it's a pretty safe assumption as they are transmitted by the same mosquito in the same population, we already studied this issue and found no difference).

So there are several things at play: 
- Does Chikungunya data allows for better prediction at early stages for Zika (I'll look into sharpness, thank you for that!)? 
- At which point in time are the predictions reliable enough to translate into public health measures?
- Depending on the uncertainty on the prior, is there a point where the Chikungunya data does not influence the inference on Zika anymore?
- I have several parameters in the final model, so how does the prior on each of them influence prediction ?

Anyway, I don't think it is (that) trivial! :)

And thanks again for a stimulating conversation!
Cheers
